summary:
We developed a space mission simulation game.
It helps people interactively learn about space missions and why rockets are built the way they are.
Space missions are a complicated subject but this project aims to help make the concept simpler to explore while not completely dumbing it dumb to the point of irrelevance
details:
What is the project

Astrix is a browser-based rocket assembly and mission-planning game built with React and Vite. Players take the role of a flight director: choose a mission, assemble a launch vehicle, balance its performance against mission constraints, and launch when the build is ready.

What the Project Does

The game presents five missions, from low-Earth-orbit resupply to lunar relay and heavy-cargo delivery. Players install components and choose factory-new or surplus hardware, then use live telemetry to compare:

  • Cost against the mission budget.
  • Preparation time against the launch deadline.
  • Thrust-to-weight ratio and delta-V against mission targets.
  • Vehicle mass and the game's reliability estimate.

The mission-control dashboard includes a rocket assembly bay, flight scene, telemetry log, mission briefings, and an in-app NASA Codex with reference tables and external resources. Campaign outcomes and the callsign are saved in browser local storage.



Challenge

The project is presented as a NASA Space Apps Challenge experience and draws on the Space Mission Design Game challenge resources. It makes mission-design trade-offs tangible through an interactive build, budget and schedule constraints, launch checks, and visible mission outcomes.

This is an educational game, not a real launch-planning tool. Its vehicle performance and flight are simplified, predefined game rules; it does not calculate real trajectories or use live NASA data. See Challenge context for the project's approach and limits.

Tools and Software

Figma - User Interface Design and Styling
VSCode - Code editor and development environment
React - Programming framework of choice
